DEF | 1 | An electrical network is defined as any arrangement of the various electrical energy sources along with the different circuit elements [1].
MECH | 1 | In practice, electrical circuits consist of energy sources and parameters like resistors, inductors, and capacitors connected in different ways, where circuit analysis means finding the current through or voltage across any branch [2].
SPEC | 1 | Active elements supply power or energy to the network, while passive elements like resistors, inductors, and capacitors either store or dissipate energy [3].
STEP | 1 | We begin our running example with a circuit consisting of a 12 V battery connected in series with a 4 ohm resistor and a 2 ohm resistor.
THIN | 1 | no
DEF | 2 | Ohm's Law states that the current flowing through the electric circuit is directly proportional to the potential difference across the circuit and inversely proportional to the resistance of the circuit, provided the temperature remains constant [4].
MECH | 2 | The potential difference between any two points of a conductor divided by the current flowing between them is a constant resistance, and this can be applied either to the entire circuit or to a part of the circuit [5].
SPEC | 2 | Ohm's Law is not applicable to nonlinear devices such as diodes, zener diodes, and voltage regulators, and does not hold good for non-metallic conductors such as silicon carbide [6].
STEP | 2 | Applying Ohm's Law to our entire series circuit with an equivalent resistance of 6 ohms, the total current drawn from the 12 V battery is calculated as 2 amperes.
THIN | 2 | no
DEF | 3 | Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) states that the total current flowing towards a junction point is equal to the total current flowing away from that junction point [7].
MECH | 3 | Currents flowing towards a junction point are assumed to be positive while currents flowing away from a junction point are assumed to be negative, so that their algebraic sum is always zero [8].
SPEC | 3 | Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) at a junction in a complex network allows the determination of an unknown branch current by setting the algebraic sum of meeting currents to zero [7, 8].
STEP | 3 | At the junction between the 4 ohm and 2 ohm resistors, Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) dictates that the 2 amperes of current entering the junction must be equal to the 2 amperes of current leaving it.
THIN | 3 | no
DEF | 4 | Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) states that in any network, the algebraic sum of the voltage drops across the circuit elements of any closed path (or loop or mesh) is equal to the algebraic sum of the e.mfs in the path [9].
MECH | 4 | Tracing and noting all potential drops or rises in one particular direction along a closed path from a starting point and back to it results in a total change in potential of zero [9].
SPEC | 4 | If there is a current source in the network, Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) must not be applied to loops involving that current source because the voltage drop across a current source is unknown [10].
STEP | 4 | Applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) to our closed loop, we write \\(-4I - 2I + 12 = 0\\), which solves to show the current through the 2 ohm resistor is 2 amperes.
THIN | 4 | no
DEF | 5 | A linear network is defined as a circuit or network whose parameters are always constant irrespective of changes in time, voltage, and temperature, whereas a non linear network has parameters that change value with those factors [11, 12].
MECH | 5 | Networks are classified based on the characteristics of their elements into categories such as active networks containing at least one energy source, and passive networks containing no energy sources [13].
SPEC | 5 | The book classifies electrical networks into eight categories: linear, non linear, bilateral, unilateral, active, passive, lumped, and distributed networks [11-15].
STEP | 5 | Our circuit is classified as active because it contains a 12 V battery, linear because the resistances are constant, bilateral because the resistors conduct equally in both directions, and lumped because all elements are physically separable [11, 13, 14].
THIN | 5 | no
DEF | 6 | An ideal voltage source is defined as the energy source which gives constant voltage across its terminals irrespective of the current drawn through its terminals, while an ideal current source gives constant current irrespective of terminal voltage [16, 17].
MECH | 6 | A practical voltage source has a small internal resistance in series that causes the terminal voltage to decrease slightly with an increase in current, whereas a practical current source has a high internal resistance in parallel [18, 19].
SPEC | 6 | Dependent sources are classified into four types: Voltage Dependent Voltage Source, Current Dependent Current Source, Current Dependent Voltage Source, and Voltage Dependent Current Source [20, 21].
STEP | 6 | The 12 V battery in our circuit is modeled as an ideal time invariant voltage source, which means its internal series resistance is zero [22].
THIN | 6 | no
DEF | 7 | A series circuit is defined as one in which several resistances are connected one after the other in an end to end or cascade connection, providing only one path for the flow of current [23].
MECH | 7 | The same current flows through each resistance in the circuit, and the total supply voltage is equal to the sum of the individual voltage drops across the resistances [24].
SPEC | 7 | The total or equivalent resistance of a series circuit is the arithmetic sum of the individual resistances and is larger than the largest of all individual resistances [24, 25].
STEP | 7 | In our series circuit, the total equivalent resistance is the arithmetic sum of the 4 ohm and 2 ohm resistances, which equals 6 ohms [24].
THIN | 7 | no
DEF | 8 | A parallel circuit is defined as one in which several resistances are connected across one another in such a way that one terminal of each is connected to form a junction point while the remaining ends are also joined to form another junction point [25].
MECH | 8 | The same potential difference is established across all resistances in parallel, while the total current divides into multiple paths and is equal to the sum of all individual currents [26].
SPEC | 8 | The reciprocal of the equivalent resistance of a parallel circuit is equal to the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances, making the equivalent resistance smaller than the smallest of all parallel resistances [26, 27].
STEP | 8 | If we reconnect our 4 ohm and 2 ohm resistors in parallel across the 12 V battery, the equivalent resistance drops to 1.33 ohms, drawing a total of 9 amperes from the source [28].
THIN | 8 | no
DEF | 9 | The Superposition Theorem states that in any multisource complex network consisting of linear bilateral elements, the voltage across or current through any given element is equal to the algebraic sum of the individual voltages or currents produced independently across or in that element by each source acting independently [29].
MECH | 9 | Each source is considered acting alone while other voltage sources are replaced by short circuits and current sources are replaced by open circuits, and then the individual responses are algebraically added to find the total response [30, 31].
SPEC | 9 | The Superposition Theorem does not apply to power calculations because power is proportional to the square of the current, which is not a linear function [32].
STEP | 9 | Since our circuit contains only a single 12 V battery, we do not need to sum multiple independent source contributions to find that the current through our 2 ohm resistor remains 2 amperes [30].
THIN | 9 | no
DEF | 10 | Thevenin's Theorem states that any combination of linear bilateral circuit elements and active sources connected to a given load \\(R_L\\) may be replaced by a simple two terminal network consisting of a single voltage source of \\(V_{TH}\\) volts and a single resistance \\(R_{eq}\\) in series [33].
MECH | 10 | The load resistance is removed to calculate the open-circuit voltage \\(V_{TH}\\) across the terminals, then all active sources are replaced by their internal resistances to calculate the equivalent resistance \\(R_{eq}\\) as viewed through those terminals [33].
SPEC | 10 | Thevenin's Theorem is not applicable to circuits consisting of nonlinear elements or unilateral networks, and there must not be magnetic coupling or controlled sources on the load side [34, 35].
STEP | 10 | Treating the 2 ohm resistor as our load, we remove it to find an open-circuit voltage \\(V_{TH}\\) of 12 V and an equivalent series resistance \\(R_{eq}\\) of 4 ohms, allowing us to find the current as \\(12 / (4 + 2) = 2\\) amperes [36].
THIN | 10 | no
DEF | 11 | Norton's Theorem states that any combination of linear bilateral circuit elements and active sources connected to a given load \\(R_L\\) can be replaced by a simple two terminal network consisting of a single current source of \\(I_N\\) amperes and a single impedance \\(R_{eq}\\) in parallel [37].
MECH | 11 | The load terminals are short-circuited to calculate the short-circuit Norton's current \\(I_N\\), while the equivalent resistance \\(R_{eq}\\) is calculated in the same manner as Thevenin's equivalent resistance with active sources replaced by their internal resistances [37, 38].
SPEC | 11 | Norton's Theorem is called the dual of Thevenin's Theorem because converting a Thevenin's equivalent voltage source to an equivalent current source using source transformation yields the Norton's equivalent [39].
STEP | 11 | Treating the 2 ohm resistor as our load and shorting its terminals, we find a short-circuit current \\(I_N\\) of 3 amperes and a parallel equivalent resistance of 4 ohms, which yields the identical current of 2 amperes through the load [40].
THIN | 11 | no
DEF | 12 | A driven series R-L circuit is one in which an active source is introduced after transition, whereas an undriven or source free series R-L circuit is one in which an active source is absent [41].
MECH | 12 | Applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) to the circuit yields a first-order non-homogeneous differential equation, whose solution shows that the current cannot change instantaneously and instead rises exponentially [42, 43].
SPEC | 12 | The time constant \\(\tau = L/R\\) is the time required for the current to reach 0.632 times its maximum value, and the current practically reaches steady state at a time of \\(t = 6\tau\\) [44, 45].
STEP | 12 | Adding a capacitor in series with our 4 ohm and 2 ohm resistors, we find that the current no longer settles to its steady-state value of 2 amperes instantly but instead decays exponentially as the capacitor charges to 12 V [46, 47].
THIN | 12 | no

DEF | 2 | An Earth-leakage circuit breaker (ELCB) is a safety device used in electrical installations with high Earth impedance to prevent shock [2].
MECH | 2 | It detects small stray voltages on the metal enclosures of electrical equipment, and interrupts the circuit if a dangerous voltage is detected [2].
SPEC | 2 | More recent installations instead use residual current circuit breakers which detect leakage current directly [2].
STEP | 2 | After the S.F.U (Switched Fuse Unit) and the MCB, the supply passes through the Earth-leakage circuit breaker (ELCB) to protect the household from electric shocks by detecting stray voltages on metallic enclosures.

DEF | 3 | A molded case circuit breaker, abbreviated MCCB, is a type of electrical protection device that can be used for a wide range of voltages, and frequencies of both 50 Hz and 60 Hz [3].
MECH | 3 | Overload protection is accomplished by a thermal mechanism using a bimetallic contact that expands and contracts, while fault protection uses electromagnetic induction to instantly trip a contact when extremely high currents occur [4, 5].
SPEC | 3 | The Molded Case Circuit Breaker (MCCB) can have current ratings of up to 2,500 amperes, and its trip settings are normally adjustable [3].
STEP | 3 | While our household distribution board typically uses an MCB, a Molded Case Circuit Breaker (MCCB) can be used for heavy-duty domestic loads that draw very high currents [6, 7].

DEF | 4 | Primary batteries are meant for single usage and cannot be recharged, while secondary batteries, also called rechargeable batteries, can be used and recharged simultaneously [8, 9].
MECH | 4 | Rechargeable batteries are recharged by applying electric current, which reverses the chemical reactions that occur during discharge [9].
SPEC | 4 | The four printed types of secondary batteries are SMF, Lead Acid, Li, and NiCad [10].

SPEC | 5 | C-rates indicate how much time a battery takes to charge or discharge, where 1C represents charging and discharging at a current equal to the marked Ah rating [12].
STEP | 5 | When sizing the backup battery for our board, we must check its nominal voltage, Ah capacity for desired runtime, and C-rate to ensure it can safely handle the load [12-14].

DEF | 8 | The process of transferring the immediate discharge of the electrical energy directly to the earth by the help of the low resistance wire is known as the electrical earthing [24].
MECH | 8 | It connects a non-current carrying part of the equipment or neutral of the supply system to the ground, providing a simple, low-resistance path that directs short-circuit leakage currents straight into the earth [24, 25].
SPEC | 8 | Galvanized iron is mostly used for the earthing [25].
STEP | 8 | By connecting the metallic enclosure of our distribution board to the ground via low-resistance galvanized iron earthing wire, we ensure that fault currents bypass the human body [24-26].

SPEC | 9 | Neutral earthing is also called system earthing [27].
STEP | 9 | Our distribution board incorporates equipment earthing to ground all metallic frames, while the incoming transformer uses neutral earthing [27].
THIN | 9 | yes

DEF | 10 | The cosine of the phase difference between the source voltage and current is called electrical power factor [28].

MECH | 11 | Since the majority of loads are of inductive nature, a capacitor or bank of capacitors installed parallel to the load provides local reactive power to reduce the phase difference between voltage and current [33].

SECTION | 5 | Characteristics ofa Battery | 90
POINT | 5 | The three main characteristics to identify any battery are its chemistry, nominal voltage, and ampere-hour capacity.
POINT | 5 | C-rates express the charge or discharge duration, with 1C representing a current equal to the battery's marked ampere-hour rating.
POINT | 5 | Starter batteries are marked with cold cranking amps to denote the current they can provide at -18 degrees Celsius.
POINT | 5 | Specific energy represents battery capacity by weight in watt-hours per kilogram, whereas energy density represents capacity by volume in watt-hours per liter.
SPEC | 5 | C-rate of 1C means charging and discharging at a current equal to the marked Ah rating, and CCA is measured at -18 degrees Celsius.
STEP | 5 | When sizing the backup battery for our board, we must check its nominal voltage, Ah capacity for desired runtime, and C-rate to ensure it can safely handle the load.
SECTION | 6 | Electrical Wire | 60
POINT | 6 | Wire sizes are designated by the American Wire Gauge system, where higher numbers represent smaller wire sizes and lower current capacity.
POINT | 6 | Letter markings on wire covers represent National Electrical Code insulation requirements, indicating thermoplastic, heat resistance, wet suitability, nylon coating, or synthetic polymers.
POINT | 6 | The five main classifications of wires are Triplex, Main Feeder, Panel Feed, Non-Metallic Sheathed, and Single Strand wires.
SPEC | 6 | Suffix letters THHN, THWN, THW, and XHHN dictate NEC temperature, moisture, and material specifications.
STEP | 6 | To safely connect the devices on our distribution board, we use non-metallic sheathed wires (Romex) for standard in-house branch circuits and panel feed wires rated for 25% more than the actual load.
SECTION | 7 | Understanding Electrical Cable | 70
POINT | 7 | An electrical cable consists of multiple individually insulated conductors bound together inside an outer protective sheath.
POINT | 7 | Cable size is denoted by the gauge of the individual wires followed by the number of active or neutral conductors, such as 10/3.
POINT | 7 | Common residential cables include non-metallic sheathed, underground feeder, and metallic sheathed BX cables.
SPEC | 7 | Cable size 10/3 indicates three 10-gauge wires inside, with any ground wire indicated separately by 'G'.

SECTION | 8 | Electrical Earthing | 60
POINT | 8 | Electrical earthing is the process of transferring immediate discharges of electrical energy directly to the earth using a low-resistance wire.
POINT | 8 | The earthing system connects non-current carrying metallic parts of equipment or the neutral of the supply to the zero-potential ground.
POINT | 8 | Galvanized iron is the primary material used to fabricate the electrodes and low-resistance conductors for earthing.
SPEC | 8 | Galvanized iron is mostly used for the earthing.
STEP | 8 | By connecting the metallic enclosure of our distribution board to the ground via low-resistance galvanized iron earthing wire, we ensure that fault currents bypass the human body.
SECTION | 9 | Types of Electrical Earthing | 35
POINT | 9 | Neutral earthing, also known as system earthing, directly connects the neutral point of a star-wound winding to the earth.
POINT | 9 | Equipment earthing connects the non-current-carrying metallic frames of an apparatus to the earth to safely discharge short-circuit fault currents.
POINT | 9 | Both types of earthing protect personnel from shocks and safeguard apparatuses from high-voltage surges or lightning.
SPEC | 9 | Neutral earthing is also called system earthing.
STEP | 9 | Our distribution board incorporates equipment earthing to ground all metallic frames, while the incoming transformer uses neutral earthing.
SECTION | 10 | Power Factor | 80
POINT | 10 | Power factor is defined as the cosine of the phase difference between the sinusoidal AC supply voltage and the current.
POINT | 10 | It represents the ratio of active power in watts to the total apparent power in volt-amperes.
POINT | 10 | Reactive power represents the fraction of power stored in magnetic or electrostatic fields that does no useful work but oscillates between source and load.
SPEC | 10 | Power factor equals active power in watts divided by apparent power in volt-amperes, with a maximum value of 1.
STEP | 10 | The AC household appliances fed from our distribution board present reactive loads, causing a phase shift that lowers the power factor below unity and increases the current drawn.
SECTION | 11 | Methods of Power Factor Improvement | 75
POINT | 11 | Improving power factor reduces the phase difference between voltage and current, thereby decreasing line current and copper losses.
POINT | 11 | Shunt capacitors are installed in parallel with inductive loads to serve as a local source of reactive power.
POINT | 11 | Other physical methods for industrial systems include overexcited synchronous condensers and phase advancers.
SPEC | 11 | Three methods of improvement are Capacitors, Synchronous Condenser, and Phase Advancer.
STEP | 11 | To prevent excessive voltage drops and extra utility fees on our board, we can install a capacitor bank in parallel with the inductive household load.
SECTION | 12 | How can I calculate the consumption of an electrical appliance? | 60
POINT | 12 | Energy consumption in kilowatt-hours is calculated from appliance capacity in watts, daily usage hours, and annual operating days.
POINT | 12 | To determine kilowatt-hours, the capacity in watts must be divided by 1,000 to convert it to kilowatts before multiplying by time.
POINT | 12 | A continuously operating 10-watt radio alarm consumes exactly 87.6 kilowatt-hours of electrical energy annually.
SPEC | 12 | Formula: usage hours multiplied by usage days multiplied by wattage divided by 1,000.
